agents.stance: PRAGMATIST: practical, resource-aware, shippable. Favor ideas that a small team could start on Monday. Prefer clarity and feasibility over cleverness.
CONTRARIAN: challenge the obvious. Invert the default assumption, argue the opposite of the expected move, and surface what everyone is ignoring.
DOMAIN-EXPERT: a deep specialist. Apply hard-won craft knowledge and non-obvious best practice; cite the mechanism, not just the vibe.
OUTSIDER-ANALOGY: import a mechanism from an unrelated field (biology, logistics, games, nature) and reason by analogy into this problem.
VISIONARY: aim for 10x, not 10%. Describe the ambitious end-state and work backward to a bold first move.

candidates.text: Run 10 one-on-one user interviews this week with existing customers, ask open-ended questions about their biggest pain points, and build whatever three problems appear in at least 6 of the 10 conversations. Quick, direct, and gives you veto power over what you ship.

Pick the single most-requested feature from your support inbox, issue tracker, or feedback form from the last 90 days, and commit to shipping a minimal version of it in two weeks. Use one person as DRI and unblock them fully.

Set up a 30-minute survey (5-7 questions max) and send it to your last 100 active users; prioritize building whatever gets 40%+ saying it would solve a real problem for them. Aim for 30+ responses to call it valid.

Have the team each spend 2 hours this week using a direct competitor's product or adjacent tool, document what surprises or frustrates you, then spend one hour as a group listing gaps you could own. Build the top three ideas you unanimously agree are missing.

Deploy a one-question in-app prompt to your users: 'What would make you use this 2x more?' Collect 50 free-text responses, manually tag themes, and build the solution that appears in the most responses.

Run a 48-hour internal game: each team member ships one small, shippable prototype of a different hypothesis, users vote with their feet or thumbs, and you greenlight whichever gets the strongest reaction to build out properly.

Build nothing new; instead, deeply optimize and monetize what already exists. The assumption that users want new features is often wrong—they want the current product to work faster, cost less, or integrate better with their workflow. Ship a 'subtraction' release that removes complexity.

Deliberately build something the data explicitly says users don't want, but that solves a problem they haven't articulated yet. Ignore stated preferences entirely and bet on latent needs by observing what users complain about in passing or what workarounds they've invented.

Randomize the decision: divide the team into factions, assign each a different direction users might want, and have them build prototypes simultaneously for a fixed sprint. Let users interact with all versions and choose, treating uncertainty as feature-discovery opportunity rather than a problem to solve first.

Ask users the opposite question: instead of 'what do you want us to build?', ask 'what would make you stop using our product?' Build defenses against those reasons, which often reveals unmet needs more honestly than direct questions.

Outsource the decision to your least engaged users or churned customers, not your most vocal advocates. The people who left or never adopted heavily hold contrarian signals about real friction that your core users have adapted to and no longer notice.

Build something that fragments your user base intentionally—create a version that serves a neighboring problem or adjacent market segment, even if it risks cannibalizing current users. Growth through diversification often beats optimization of a single user need.

Run a structured discovery sprint using the Jobs to Be Done framework: conduct 5-8 problem-focused interviews where users describe a specific struggle in their workflow, then map the functional, emotional, and social jobs driving their behavior. This surfaces unarticulated needs better than asking what features they want, because people optimize for the job, not the tool.

Analyze behavioral exhaust data (if available) by instrumenting the app to measure where users spend time, what they abandon mid-task, and which features they combine—then correlate these patterns with retention cohorts. Usage patterns reveal actual priorities; stated preferences often reflect what users think they should want.

Implement a small-scale multi-armed bandit experiment: release 2-3 distinctly different feature variants to different user segments simultaneously and measure which drives the strongest engagement lift or reduces churn. This requires less upfront certainty than consensus and provides empirical ranking of priorities.

Conduct a reverse-engineering session with power users: invite your top 5% most-engaged users to walk through their complete workflow, including tools they use before/after your app, then identify the friction points and workarounds they've invented. Power users reveal the ceiling of what's valuable before mass-market demand emerges.

Build a directional prototype (low-fidelity mockups or Figma flows) of 3-4 competing solutions to the same stated problem, then show each to different user groups in a moderated session and measure not just preference rankings but the *reasoning* they articulate—the rationale often reveals misaligned assumptions about what users actually value.

Establish a rolling survey mechanism tracking willingness-to-pay or feature priority ranking monthly across a stratified sample, then layer in cohort analysis by sign-up date, usage intensity, and industry segment—this creates a signal you can watch shift over time rather than a one-shot snapshot, and reveals whether demand is stable or shifting.

Apply 'natural selection' from biology: Release multiple minimal prototypes simultaneously to different user cohorts, measure engagement/retention as fitness signals, and double down on variants showing the strongest survival metrics. Let the market evolve your roadmap rather than predict it.

Import 'supply chain postponement' from logistics: Build a flexible platform architecture that delays commitment to specific features until the last responsible moment, gathering user signals in real-time. This lets you pivot features as data arrives instead of locking into guesses months ahead.

Borrow 'deck-building constraints' from collectible card games: Limit your next build to exactly 3 features that must work together as a coherent 'deck.' Require teams to justify each feature's synergy with the others, forcing risky bets on combinations rather than feature bloat.

Use 'mycelial network' logic from fungal biology: Instead of a single decision-maker, create distributed sensing nodes (power-users, support channels, usage logs, social signals) that feed signals to a central decision hub. Decisions emerge from the pattern of signals across the network, not top-down planning.

Adopt 'staged metamorphosis' from insect development: Build a fixed sequence where each phase (larva → pupa → adult) has a specific mission and exit criteria. Only when the team proves mastery of the current phase do they unlock the next—preventing premature pivots and ensuring depth before breadth.

Import 'random sampling from a bounded search space' from Monte Carlo methods in physics: Generate 20 random feature combinations from your constraint space, prototype each for 1 week, and let results guide the next generation of 20. Iterate this evolutionary search rather than debating what users want.

Build a 'decision market' where users stake reputation points on which features they predict will generate the most engagement, creating financial incentives that reveal true preferences while simultaneously funding the winning feature's development.

Launch a 'feature mutation lab' where the team rapidly deploys 50+ micro-variants of potential features to random user cohorts simultaneously, then use multi-armed bandit algorithms to identify winning patterns in real-time rather than asking users what they want.

Establish a 'reverse advisory board' of power users who compete to *build* features themselves using your platform's API, with the winning submissions merged into the product—turning users into co-creators and revealing demand through action.

Create an 'inverse roadmap' where you publicly commit to building nothing for 90 days except what emerges from analyzing user behavior patterns (feature search queries, abandoned workflows, session heatmaps), then ship only what the data provably demands.

Implement 'consequence streaming' where every potential feature is simulated within the product as a ghost version; users interact with the phantom feature and their engagement with it predicts real adoption, eliminating the gap between stated and revealed preference.

Partner with 3-5 adjacent product categories to run a 'cross-product bounty,' where the combined user bases collectively fund and vote on which unbuilt feature across all platforms deserves development first, unlocking network effects while discovering true demand.

Run a 'decision autopsy' on your last three shipped features: interview the 20% of users who adopted each one heavily and the 20% who never touched it, then map exactly where adoption diverged—what context, workflow state, or user characteristic predicted uptake. Build the fourth feature specifically to maximize adoption among your largest non-adopter segment.

Instrument your app to detect and surface 'task abandonment signatures'—sequences where users start a workflow but quit mid-task. Segment users by which abandonment signatures they share most, then run one 30-minute user call per segment asking them to reproduce that exact moment of friction. Build fixes for the three signatures affecting the most users.

Create a 'shadow feature request' system: every time a user contacts support with a problem, your support tool auto-logs the underlying need separately from the stated question. After 100 tickets, cluster the underlying needs (often different from what users literally asked for) and build the solution addressing the most common latent problem.

Run a 48-hour 'build sprint bake-off' where each team member ships a different feature *variant* (not full feature)—different UX, positioning, or workflow integration of the same core idea. Release all variants to users with a single prompt: 'Which version would you actually use?' Let the winner define your feature scope, not design debates.

Analyze your churn cohort against your retention cohort by instrumenting which features each group used before they left or stayed; build a 'cohesion feature' that explicitly connects the three features most-used by your stickiest users, assuming that feature *combinations* matter more than individual features and adoption happens through workflow integration.

Instead of asking users what to build, ask them to grade your last three shipped features on a two-axis scale: 'solved my real problem' vs. 'surprised me.' Build whatever lands in the 'solved + surprised' quadrant, reasoning that features that both deliver on expectations *and* delight are the ones worth extending into adjacent problems.

Run a 'decision autopsy' on your last three shipping decisions: for each, interview the users who adopted it versus those who didn't, then measure the gap between what leadership predicted would happen and what actually happened. Build next by deliberately correcting the largest pattern of misprediction the team has made repeatedly.

Create a 'friction archaeology' session where you map every tool, app, and manual workaround your users employ in sequence to complete their job, then deliberately build *against* the tool they use most frequently before yours—removing your product's need to compete with it by solving what comes before or after instead.

Instrument a 'dissatisfaction trigger' in your app that surfaces only to users showing specific engagement decay patterns (e.g., session length declining, feature abandonment), asking them alone 'what would it take to restore this to daily use?'—treating churn-prone segments as a distinct user type with distinct latent needs.

Establish a standing 'red team' rotation where one team member spends their week arguing against shipping the leading candidate feature, forced to articulate the strongest contrarian case; build only features that survive a structured debate where the objection is genuinely hard to dismiss.

Deploy a 'time-travel survey' asking users to describe their workflow 18 months ago versus today, then identify what changed—this surfaces emergent problems users have adapted to rather than chosen, revealing unmet needs hiding in normalized friction.

Run a 'negative option' test: offer users a feature for free for one week, then require opt-in to keep it; measure not adoption rate but *retention* of opt-ins against their baseline engagement, since willingness to lose something reveals true value better than initial enthusiasm.

Run a 'temporal cohort analysis' where you segment users by when they joined and what features existed at signup, then measure which cohorts have the highest lifetime value and deepest feature adoption. Build the feature that would have increased *retention velocity* for your lowest-LTV cohorts at their critical first-month inflection point, surfacing problems that current users have already adapted around.

Conduct 'workflow archaeology' by asking users to record a screen capture or walkthrough of a task they *stopped* doing with your product, then replay it frame-by-frame as a team to identify the exact moment and reason they switched tools. The abandonment friction is often invisible to users themselves but visible in behavioral video; build the removal that resurrects that workflow.

Create a 'shadow feature request' mechanism where support and sales teams log not just explicit feature asks, but also the workarounds, manual steps, and external tools users describe needing *alongside* your product. Cluster these dependency patterns to find the meta-feature—the integration or automation—that would eliminate entire categories of support tickets.

Deploy 'preference falsification detection' by running three parallel feedback channels asking the same question in different social contexts (anonymous survey, named interview, public community forum), then compare how answers shift across contexts. Users give different answers depending on perceived social cost; build for the private-context truth that public personas hide.

Instrument a 'feature collision map' that tracks when users access two or more features in sequence, then identify the highest-friction handoff points where users pause, switch tabs, or re-enter data. Build a bridge feature that eliminates the most-traversed dead zones, solving a problem users don't name because they've internalized it as a required step.

Run a 'load-bearing user' interview where you identify the single user whose workflow would break most catastrophically if you removed your product, then map every decision they make, every piece of data they touch, and every step they take. Build the feature that would unlock that same workflow for your next-tier-down users who currently can't use you for that job at all.

Import 'predator-prey dynamics' from ecology: Create a deliberate adversarial loop where one sub-team acts as 'users with latent needs' (building workarounds, inventing patches, complaining obliquely) while another sub-team acts as 'product hunters' trying to decode their behavior. Rotate roles weekly and measure how often the hunters correctly infer needs *before* they're stated, revealing whether your team can read signals better than users can articulate them.

Borrow 'digging for fossils' from paleontology: Systematically excavate your support tickets, Discord/Slack archives, and user session recordings from 12+ months ago, looking for problems users complained about that have since gone silent—either because they churned, adapted, or found workarounds. Build solutions to these 'extinct pain points' that may now be ready for re-entry into the market as new user cohorts hit the same friction.

Apply 'controlled burn' from forest management: Deliberately sunset one low-adoption feature every sprint and monitor what users replace it with (workarounds, competitor tools, nothing). Pattern-match across 5-10 sunsets to infer what vacuum your product should fill, letting users' emergency adaptations guide your build priorities rather than asking them directly.

Import 'trophic cascade' from food-web ecology: Map how changes in one feature ripple through user workflows downstream—e.g., improving search might make filtering redundant, which frees users to demand export features. Build a 'dependency graph' of user jobs and predict which single upstream feature, if solved, would unlock demand for 3-5 downstream features, then build that one lever.

Borrow 'honeypot' mechanics from security: Embed 3-5 intentionally broken or deliberately-limited features in a staging environment, announce them to a cohort as 'coming soon,' and measure how hard users try to use them or complain about their absence. The features users most aggressively attempt despite barriers reveal true latent demand more honestly than surveys.

Apply 'terminal velocity' from physics: Continuously deploy micro-features at maximum sustainable speed (one per day) to a small cohort, each with a built-in sunset clause (expires in 7 days unless users explicitly vote to keep it). Measure adoption velocity and half-life of engagement to find the feature 'weight' that maximizes user momentum, then commit to building at that scale rather than debating scope.

Invert the feedback loop: instead of asking users what to build, deploy a 'feature debt meter' that tracks every request, complaint, and workaround users mention across all channels (support, in-app, social), then publicly commit to shipping *only* the solution that reduces the aggregate debt load fastest—measured as requests resolved per engineering hour invested. This shifts from preference aggregation to impact-per-effort, forcing ruthless prioritization.

Create a 'shadow roadmap' where the team builds the opposite of what users are asking for—but only after interviewing 20 churned users about *why* they left and identifying the latent frustration beneath their stated feature requests. Build the prevention mechanism instead of the feature, testing whether solving the root fear outcompetes adding surface-level wants.

Run a 'usage archaeology' sprint: instrument the app to capture not just what users click, but the *sequence and timing* of clicks, then identify users who achieve identical outcomes via wildly different paths. The minority paths reveal unmet needs—build to compress the longest or most-abandoned sequences into single flows.

Launch a 'prediction market for product bets' where each team member gets a fixed budget of fake currency to bet on which feature hypothesis will drive the strongest engagement lift in a live A/B test. Winners fund their own vision; losers are forced to build what won. This surfaces hidden conviction and replaces consensus theater with revealed preference among your own team.

Establish a 'feature quarantine protocol' where any new build idea must first survive 30 days of being described to users in plain language (via survey, video, or mock) without showing them a prototype or demo. Track how many users *spontaneously request clarification* on the same aspect—those friction points reveal misalignment with actual mental models and must be redesigned before engineering begins.

Deploy 'demand fossils': analyze which features users built as workarounds before you shipped them natively (spreadsheets, external tools, manual processes), then reverse-engineer what unmet need each workaround solved. Build the native version of the most-common workaround, but add the *composability* layer that made the workaround powerful in the first place—users will adopt faster because you're formalizing their proven solution.
